422.history: A hill-fort east of the vein with a double bank, raised in the four thousand two hundred and seventy-fourth year by households who owed nothing to Dùn ìseal and asked leave of no one. They shared out the labour, and afterward the ground within, by households and not by standing; a family that sent no hands was left outside the second bank and asked within a generation to be let in on the same terms. Ailis carried seal-skins from here to the ford, and Catrìona of the king's blood gave the eastern households ground there asking no oath. In the four thousand five hundred and twentieth year the king sent Niall Òg to bid Dùn dhearg come in to him, and Fearghal Donn sent him back with nothing. From that year the spears of the east were gathered here, and under Artair mac Fhearghail the host mustered along the river below the fort in the last days of an Lùnastal, meaning to hold the crossing.
422.known_for: the double bank, and the refusal

12.history: A stony crossing in the south-eastern hills where wild cattle came down to drink. Households settled it in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-fifth year and reared the calves born on the near bank apart from the wild herd, until within three generations that ford's cattle were spoken of the length of the coast as the best in the hills. The settlers came from the valleys under Dùn ìseal and kept the sharing before the storms, bringing calves as their surplus rather than grain. Their herds were driven to the ford in the autumns, and in the years of the waiting below the hill they sold beasts to the camps of the king's kin.

269.history: A damp hill in the north-west settled in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-eighth year by households who drained it with ditches before they built, and grazed its wet slopes with sheep. The ditches carried water through the rest of the age, and the households traded with the mill-folk of Muileann àrsaidh below them. The ditches were cut to a line the eldest of the settlers paced out alone over a whole wet winter, and no household afterward moved a ditch without the others walking it first. They measured their coal by the cup like every hearth of the hills.

17.history: A fishing settlement on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east, taken up in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-eighth year by households who lived by the fish of its sheltered pools. They built their houses in two rows facing each other across a single trodden way, so that a neighbour's fire might be borrowed without crossing open ground in the rain: the oldest street any teller remembers on Dia-thìr. The two rows faced each other close enough for a word to cross between doors, and the settlement kept its sharing in the trodden way itself, each household setting out its surplus at its own door to be divided by the count of mouths before the storms.
